choices.text: It is induced by brief upper-limb cuff ischemia, and trials show mixed results
It has been proven to reduce mortality and is now in general use
It works only by local myocardial adenosine release, without any humoral factor
It is induced by brief aortic cross-clamp occlusions before the main arrest
It is induced by intracoronary adenosine before aortic clamping

explanation.text: Remote ischemic preconditioning protects the myocardium by inducing ischemia in a **distant organ** (e.g., arm skeletal muscle); in cardiac surgery it is done with **upper-limb cuff** cycles, and clinical trials have produced **mixed results**.

steps.text: Upper-limb cuff inflated to **200 mmHg** for **3 to 5 minutes**

items: Its **simpler application** to cardiac surgery makes it the object of numerous clinical trials
Distant-organ protection, and transfer of a preconditioning factor from animal to animal, suggest a **humoral factor**

explanation.text: Remote ischemic preconditioning has been implemented during cardiac surgery simply by 3- to 5-minute cycles of upper-limb cuff inflation to 200 mmHg, separated by 5 minutes of cuff deflation. Clinical trials have thus far produced mixed results.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 93

choiceNotes.b: Clinical trials have so far produced **mixed results**.
choiceNotes.c: Protection from a distant organ and a transferable factor suggest a **humoral factor**.
choiceNotes.d: Remote preconditioning uses ischemia of a **distant organ**, not of the heart itself.
choiceNotes.e: Remote preconditioning uses ischemia of a **distant organ** (e.g., arm skeletal muscle), not a drug.

questions.stem: During **controlled reperfusion**, electromechanical quiescence is maintained for the first **3 to 5 minutes**. What is the rationale?

choices.text: To allow a perfusion pressure of 100 mmHg without causing myocardial edema
To speed energy repletion, limit energy use and limit intracellular calcium
To wash out adenosine and lactic acid, which raise coronary resistance
To allow crystalloid reperfusate, which is superior to blood
To keep the myocardium cold, because reperfusate at 4°C protects best

explanation.text: Quiescence for the first **3 to 5 min** permits **more rapid repletion of energy charge**, minimizes **regional heterogeneity** of reperfusion flow, minimizes **energy expenditure** until recovery, and minimizes intracellular **calcium** accumulation.

items: Minimize persistence of myocardial **stunning** into the post-CPB period
Optimal recovery of **reversibly damaged** myocardium
**Resuscitate** myocytes that would otherwise have undergone necrosis

children: Control until recovery is essentially complete

explanation.text: Maintaining electromechanical quiescence during the first 3 to 5 minutes of reperfusion to permit more rapid repletion of myocardial energy charge
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 93

choiceNotes.e: The source does not advise a cold reperfusate; normothermia is advantageous to the normal function of enzyme systems.
choiceNotes.a: Quiescence is not described as a way to permit a high perfusion pressure.
choiceNotes.c: Adenosine and lactic acid accumulated during ischemia **lower** coronary resistance at the start of reperfusion.
choiceNotes.d: **Blood** has been shown to be superior to crystalloid as the reperfusion vehicle.

questions.stem: **Blood** is superior to crystalloid solutions as the reperfusion vehicle, in part because of its **red blood cell** component. Which property of red blood cells is stressed as important?

choices.text: Their supply of adenosine for rapid ATP repletion
Their release of nitric oxide to dilate the coronaries
Their abundant content of oxygen-derived free radical scavengers
Their oxygen transport capacity at a hematocrit above 0.30
Their high calcium content, which restores contractility quickly

explanation.text: Red blood cells contain **abundant oxygen-derived free radical scavengers**; the advantage of blood **may not relate** to the oxygen transport capacity of red cells.

explanation.caption: Why blood is the better reperfusate
head: Component
Contribution

explanation.text: Because blood carries natural free radical scavengers, using blood as the reperfusate **appears to obviate** the need for added scavenger agents in clinical cardiac surgery.
Among other things, red blood cells contain abundant oxygen-derived free radical scavengers, which are important. The minimal effective hematocrit level in the reperfusate is 0.15 to 0.20.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 93

choiceNotes.d: The advantage **may not relate** to oxygen transport, and the minimal effective hematocrit is only **0.15 to 0.20**.
choiceNotes.e: Reperfusate calcium should be **low** to minimize calcium influx into damaged myocytes.
choiceNotes.a: Red cells are not described as an adenosine source; the stressed property is their free radical scavenger content.
choiceNotes.b: This is not the red cell property stressed by the source.

questions.stem: A surgeon wants to change the **cellular content** of the blood reperfusate to reduce reperfusion injury. Which change is supported by the source?

choices.text: Replacing blood with an acellular crystalloid reperfusate
Raising the reperfusate hematocrit above 0.40 for oxygen delivery
Diluting the reperfusate hematocrit to below 0.10
Depleting leukocytes from the reperfusate by filtration
Removing red cells to leave an acellular plasma reperfusate

explanation.text: **Activated leukocytes** play an important role in reperfusion damage; **depleting leukocytes by filtration** reduces reperfusion injury **considerably**.

items: Leukocyte filters are commercially available for **pediatric and adult** CPB circuits
Keep **blood** as the vehicle (superior to crystalloid)
Minimal effective hematocrit in the reperfusate: **0.15 to 0.20**

explanation.text: Depletion of leukocytes from the blood reperfusate (by filtration) reduces reperfusion injury considerably.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 93

choiceNotes.a: Blood as the reperfusion vehicle has been shown to be **superior** to crystalloid solutions.
choiceNotes.b: The advantage of blood may not relate to oxygen transport; the minimal effective hematocrit is **0.15 to 0.20**.
choiceNotes.c: Below 0.10 is under the minimal effective hematocrit of **0.15 to 0.20**.
choiceNotes.e: The advantage of blood is due in part to its **red blood cell** component (abundant free radical scavengers).

questions.stem: After ischemic injury, **repletion of ATP** is delayed. Which mechanism does the source give for this delay?

choices.text: Adenosine is presumably converted to inosine and washed out of cells
Hyperkalemic reperfusion blocks the cellular uptake of adenosine
Low reperfusion pressure prevents adenosine from reaching the myocytes
Excess calcium in the reperfusate directly degrades newly formed ATP
Leukocytes consume the ATP precursors carried in the reperfusate

explanation.text: The delay may relate to **lack of adenosine**, an important component in rebuilding ATP stores, because it is presumably **converted to inosine** and **washed out** of cells during reperfusion.

steps.text: Lack of adenosine to rebuild ATP -> **delayed ATP repletion**

explanation.text: This is the theory behind **adding adenosine during reperfusion**, which has experimental support. In contrast, **hyperkalemic reperfusion** permits **rapid** repletion of ATP.
The delay in repletion of ATP after ischemic injury may well relate to lack of availability of adenosine, an important component of the process of rebuilding ATP stores
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 94

choiceNotes.d: Low calcium is advised to limit calcium **influx** into damaged myocytes; ATP degradation by calcium is not the mechanism given.
choiceNotes.e: Leukocytes contribute to reperfusion damage, but they are not the reason given for delayed ATP repletion.
choiceNotes.b: Hyperkalemic reperfusion **permits rapid repletion** of ATP.
choiceNotes.c: Low early reperfusion pressure is not the reason the source gives for delayed ATP repletion.

questions.stem: A surgeon elects **controlled reperfusion**. Which **initial reperfusate** fits the source's recommendations?

choices.text: Blood, normal potassium, low calcium, no added buffer
Blood, potassium about 12 mmol/L, low calcium, added buffer
Crystalloid, potassium about 12 mmol/L, low calcium, added buffer
Blood, normal potassium, high calcium, added buffer
Blood, potassium about 12 mmol/L, high calcium, no added buffer

explanation.text: Initial reperfusate: **blood**, **hyperkalemic** (about **12 mmol/L**), **low calcium**, with large **buffering capacity** (Tris or histidine).

head: Component

rows: Superior to crystalloid; RBC free radical scavengers; protein buffering
Electromechanical quiescence; rapid ATP repletion; better flow
Minimize Ca^2+^ influx into damaged myocytes

explanation.text: Calcium in the **neonatal and infant** myocardium has special effects, discussed separately in the chapter.
Various buffering agents have been used, but hydroxymethyl aminomethane (Tris) and histidine have particularly favorable characteristics.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 94

choiceNotes.c: Blood as the reperfusion vehicle is **superior** to crystalloid solutions.
choiceNotes.d: Calcium should be **low**, and potassium high enough to keep the heart quiescent.
choiceNotes.e: Calcium should be **low**, and the reperfusate needs **adequate buffering capacity**.
choiceNotes.a: The initial reperfusate should be **hyperkalemic** and contain **adequate buffering capacity**.

choices.text: Until the reperfusate has fully reached normothermia
Until ATP levels have returned to normal
At least 2 to 3 minutes, and preferably 5 to 10 minutes
At least 30 seconds, and preferably 60 to 120 seconds
At least 15 minutes, and preferably 20 to 30 minutes

questions.stem: During the **first 60 to 120 seconds** of reperfusion after aortic clamping, what reperfusion pressure is prudent in clinical cardiac surgery, and why?

choices.text: About 100 mmHg, to ensure flow to the subendocardium
50 to 75 mmHg, or the preoperative diastolic pressure if lower
About 80 mmHg, to overcome high early coronary resistance
About 30 mmHg, because postischemic endothelium is easily damaged
About 30 mmHg, because early coronary flow is too low for higher pressure

explanation.text: Keep reperfusion pressure at about **30 mmHg** for the first **60–120 s**: postischemic coronary **endothelial cells are easily damaged by high reperfusion pressure**, a state rapidly reversed by gentle reperfusion.

steps.text: First 60–120 s: **~30 mmHg** (flow still large from **reactive hyperemia**)

steps.label: after
steps.text: **50–75 mmHg**, or the **preoperative diastolic** arterial pressure, whichever is lower (clinical experience at UAB)

explanation.text: Low pressure does **not** mean low flow: reactive hyperemia makes early coronary resistance very low, so flow may still be **large**.

Experimental upper limits vary (no higher than 50 mmHg vs as high as 100 mmHg), possibly from **species differences**; in a canine model, 1 h of hyperkalemic reperfusion at 80 mmHg (with electromechanical quiescence) **improved function** with no more edema than normokalemic reperfusion and rapid resumption of activity.
in clinical cardiac surgery, it is prudent to keep reperfusion pressure at about 30 mmHg for the first 60 to 120 seconds of reperfusion.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 94

choiceNotes.c: Early coronary resistance is **very low** (reactive hyperemia); the prudent initial pressure is about **30 mmHg**.
choiceNotes.e: Early flow is **large**, not low, because of reactive hyperemia.
choiceNotes.a: High early pressure damages the postischemic endothelium; about **30 mmHg** is advised initially.
choiceNotes.b: This is the pressure maintained **after** the first 60–120 s.

questions.stem: In an isolated blood-perfused canine heart **arrested in diastole** with maximal coronary vasodilation, coronary perfusion pressure was progressively reduced. What happened?

choices.text: Flow was unchanged down to 20 mmHg because of maximal vasodilation
Flow fell equally in all layers, so the inner/outer flow ratio was unchanged
Epicardial flow fell most, so the inner/outer flow ratio rose
Flow fell in all layers, and flow became more homogeneous
Subendocardial flow fell out of proportion, and flow heterogeneity increased

explanation.text: As perfusion pressure fell, **subendocardial** perfusion declined **out of proportion** to other layers (inner/outer ratio **fell**), and **heterogeneity** of flow **increased**.

explanation.title: Canine model, heart arrested in diastole

explanation.text: The source cites this model as documenting the importance of maintaining **sufficient coronary perfusion pressure** during reperfusion. Clinically (UAB), after the first 60–120 s, reperfusion pressure was kept at **50–75 mmHg** or the preoperative diastolic pressure, whichever was lower.
Note that as coronary perfusion pressure was reduced, perfusion of subendocardium progressively declined out of proportion to decline in other layers. Accordingly, the inner/outer ratio fell.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 94

choiceNotes.b: Flow did **not** fall equally; the subendocardium lost most, so the inner/outer ratio **fell**.
choiceNotes.c: The **subendocardium**, not the epicardium, lost flow out of proportion; the ratio **fell**.
choiceNotes.d: Heterogeneity of flow **increased** as pressure fell.
choiceNotes.a: Endocardial flow fell steeply from 70 to 40 mmHg, and heterogeneity rose markedly at 20 mmHg.

questions.stem: At the **beginning of reperfusion**, coronary flow is very high even at low reperfusion pressure. What primarily explains the very low coronary resistance at this time?

choices.text: Reactive hyperemia, aided by the cold myocardium
Normothermia of the reperfusate restoring enzyme function
Hyperkalemia directly dilating the epicardial coronary arteries
Myocardial cell swelling compressing the coronary vessels
Washout of adenosine and lactic acid during the ischemic period

explanation.text: Early coronary resistance is very low **primarily from reactive hyperemia**, with additive effects from the **cold myocardium** and **adenosine and lactic acid** accumulated during ischemia.

steps.text: Start: **very high flow** despite low pressure

steps.label: then
steps.text: About **150 mL/min** in adults (~100 mL/min/m^2^; ~40 mL/min/100 g)

explanation.text: That later flow is about **half** the value of normal hearts, yet appears **adequate** in the nonworking, empty heart being reperfused.

At the beginning of reperfusion, coronary resistance is very low, primarily as a result of reactive hyperemia, with additive effects from the cold temperature of the myocardium and the action of vasoactive substances
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 94

choiceNotes.d: Compression of coronary vessels (by swelling, hemorrhage, high wall tension) **raises** resistance; it does not explain very low resistance.
choiceNotes.e: Adenosine and lactic acid **accumulate** during ischemia and lower resistance; they are not washed out beforehand.
choiceNotes.b: Reperfusate temperature is not the explanation; the **cold** myocardium adds to the low resistance.
choiceNotes.c: Hyperkalemic reperfusion promotes better flow, but the **primary** cause of low early resistance is reactive hyperemia.

questions.stem: In practice, how does the **temperature of the reperfusate** behave during controlled reperfusion?

choices.text: Starts at about 37°C and is cooled to 28°C to limit energy use
Starts at about 35°C and rises to 37°C after 2 to 3 minutes
Starts at about 4°C and rises to 37°C after 10 to 20 minutes
Starts at about 27°C and rises to 35°C after 5 to 10 minutes
Stays at about 37°C from the first second of reperfusion

explanation.text: Because of the **heat exchange mechanism** in the reperfusion circuit, the reperfusate starts at about **35°C** and rises to **37°C** after **2 to 3 minutes**.
There may be advantages to this **gradual return to normothermia**; normothermia is advantageous to the normal function of **enzyme systems**.

In practice, the temperature of the reperfusate is initially about 35°C because of the characteristics of the heat exchange mechanism in the reperfusion circuit. After 2 to 3 minutes, the temperature rises to 37°C.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 95

choiceNotes.c: The reperfusate starts at about **35°C**, not 4°C, and reaches 37°C in **2 to 3 minutes**.
choiceNotes.d: It starts at about **35°C** and reaches **37°C**.
choiceNotes.e: It starts slightly below normothermia (about **35°C**) because of the heat exchanger.
choiceNotes.a: The reperfusate rises **to** 37°C; normothermia is advantageous to enzyme systems.

choices.text: Activating protein kinase C, as in preconditioning
Limiting calcium influx into damaged myocytes
Chelating iron, slowing hydroxyl radical formation from superoxide
Slowing conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to superoxide ions
Directly scavenging superoxide as superoxide dismutase does

explanation.text: **Deferoxamine** presumably **chelates iron**, slowing formation of highly damaging **hydroxyl radicals** from superoxide radicals.

explanation.caption: Agents against oxygen-derived free radicals (experimental)
head: Agent
Timing
Presumed action

explanation.text: Using **blood** as the reperfusate, with its naturally occurring free radical scavengers, appears to **obviate the need** for these agents in clinical cardiac surgery.

Deferoxamine, given just before reperfusion, is also protective in experimental models, presumably by chelating iron and slowing formation of highly damaging hydroxyl radicals from superoxide radicals.

choiceNotes.d: This is the presumed action of **allopurinol**.
choiceNotes.e: Superoxide dismutase and catalase are the **scavengers**; deferoxamine is described as an iron chelator.

questions.stem: A center uses **prolonged controlled normokalemic reperfusion** with adequate aortic root pressure. When can controlled aortic root reperfusion be discontinued by removing the aortic clamp?

choices.text: As soon as myocardial ATP levels have returned to normal
After exactly 3 minutes, as in warm terminal reperfusion
As soon as the first spontaneous beat appears
When it beats forcefully in sinus rhythm (usually 10–20 min)
As soon as the reperfusate temperature reaches 37°C

explanation.text: Continue until the heart **beats forcefully** and is in **sinus rhythm**, usually **10 to 20 minutes** after reperfusion begins; by then the heart itself can generate an **adequate coronary perfusion pressure**.

explanation.caption: Two approaches to reperfusion with the aorta clamped
head: Warm terminal reperfusion ("hot shot")
Prolonged controlled normokalemic reperfusion
rows: Until forceful beating in sinus rhythm (**10–20 min**)

items: Rationale: recovery is not complete at the end of the hyperkalemic phase (**incomplete cellular recovery**, **persisting inhomogeneity** of perfusion)
Experimentally, 10–20 min is needed for normal coronary resistance, MVO~2~, lactate and ventricular function
**ATP has not yet returned to normal** at this stage

explanation.text: In practice this prolonged reperfusion may **not be necessary**: reperfusion by pump flow with pharmacologic support may be adequate.
This should be continued until the heart beats forcefully and is in sinus rhythm. This stage usually occurs 10 to 20 minutes after the beginning of reperfusion.

1.5 mg/kg by intravenous bolus on arrival in the intensive care unit
0.15 mg/kg as a coronary sinus bolus just before aortic clamping

questions.stem: **Ischemic preconditioning** appears to stimulate potent innate cardioprotective mechanisms that attenuate ischemia-reperfusion injury. Which mechanism has been linked to this protection?

choices.text: Stimulation of myocyte adenosine receptors
Enhanced inflammatory response to reperfusion
Inhibition of myocardial protein kinase C
Increased tissue acidosis during the ischemic period
Blockade of myocyte α~1~-adrenergic receptors

choiceNotes.b: Preconditioning is linked to **reduction** of inflammatory responses to reperfusion.
choiceNotes.c: Protein kinase C, when **activated** by adenosine or phenylephrine, results in preconditioning protection.

questions.stem: In an adult, controlled reperfusion of the nonworking, empty heart has passed the initial period of very high flow. What is the usual **subsequent reperfusion flow**, and how is it judged?

choices.text: About 40 mL/min in total, too low for myocardial recovery
About 150 mL/min, about half of normal, yet it appears adequate
About 150 mL/min, about half of normal, and it is inadequate
About 600 mL/min, similar to the normal heart, and it is adequate
About 1500 mL/min, from reactive hyperemia that does not subside

choices.text: Normal coronary blood distribution with uniform subendocardial flow
Improved intracoronary collateral flow to potentially ischemic areas
Myocardial water accumulation that reduces ventricular distensibility
Coronary sinus rupture during insertion of the perfusion catheter
Hospital deaths in most of 100 isolated aortic valve replacements

explanation.text: With the heart perfused, empty and beating, **water accumulates in the myocardium** during CPB; in dog models ventricular **distensibility fell by nearly 50%** after 3 hours.

**Distribution of coronary blood** is abnormal

explanation.title: Still useful when used properly

20 minutes of controlled regional reperfusion of the LAD
Warm induction given antegrade only, for 5 minutes
An ITA graft to the LAD instead of any vein graft
A single cold cardioplegic dose with no further infusions

questions.stem: During **reoperative cardiac surgery**, more frequent cardioplegic infusions and/or a lower systemic perfusion temperature are advised. What is the reason given?

choices.text: Adhesions make the myocardium rewarm faster
Patent vein grafts block antegrade delivery
The coronary sinus cannot be cannulated
Reoperative hearts are severely hypertrophied
Patent ITA grafts must be left open

explanation.text: ==Because of adhesions, the myocardium tends to rewarm more quickly than usual==, so more frequent cardioplegia, low systemic perfusion temperature, or both are appropriate.

items: Establish cardioplegic protection **early**, usually **before mobilization** of the cardiac mass.
Antegrade and retrograde infusions are **complementary**: place the retrograde catheter accurately (minimal sharp dissection over the **acute margin of the RV**, then posterior freeing dissection).
With **saphenous vein grafts left in place**, aortic root antegrade plus retrograde infusion seems the surest way to near-optimal delivery at induction.

explanation.text: Because of adhesions, the myocardium tends to rewarm more quickly than usual.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 104

choiceNotes.b: With vein grafts in place, **antegrade root plus retrograde** infusion is the surest delivery; the stated reason for frequent dosing is faster rewarming.
choiceNotes.c: The retrograde catheter **can** be placed accurately via dissection over the acute margin of the RV.
choiceNotes.d: Hypertrophy is not the stated reason; **adhesions** cause faster rewarming.
choiceNotes.e: A patent ITA is usually **occluded**; leaving it open is only an alternative.
